questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy intern withdraws from an approved PharmD program on November 4, 2026. The school updates its registrar and the pharmacy updates its payroll file. No notice has been sent to the Massachusetts Board. What additional action is required by 247 CMR 8.01(18)?

choices.text: The intern must give the Board written notice within 14 days after withdrawing.
choices.why: Correct. Section 8.01(18) places a separate written 14-day notification duty on the pharmacy intern.

choices.text: The employer's payroll change automatically completes the intern's Board reporting duty.
choices.why: Incorrect. An internal employer record is not the intern's written notice to the Board.

choices.text: Only the pharmacy preceptor must notify the Board, within seven business days.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 8.01(18) expressly assigns the duty to the intern and states 14 days.

choices.text: No reporting is required until the person reapplies to pharmacy school.
choices.why: Incorrect. The duty is triggered by withdrawal from the approved program.

choices.text: The intern may wait until the next pharmacist-license renewal cycle.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule sets a specific 14-day deadline independent of the renewal cycle.

questions.material_novelty: The triggering event is PharmD-program withdrawal, not demographic updates or out-of-state hour credit.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the intern remains enrolled and only changes mailing address, the 8.01(18) withdrawal notice does not apply.

questions.stem: An ACPE-affiliated pharmacy school proposes awarding 80 intern hours for a new clinical demonstration project. The student's preceptor has documented every hour, but the school has not submitted a description of the project to the Massachusetts Board. What is the correct approval pathway?

choices.text: Preceptor signatures alone make any demonstration-project hours automatically creditable.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board may determine whether a described program earns credit; supervision records alone do not decide that.

choices.text: Any program is creditable without Board review when it awards fewer than 100 hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation does not create this 100-hour exemption.

choices.text: The student's NAPLEX eligibility automatically approves all demonstration-project hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. Exam eligibility is not the Board's program-credit determination.

choices.text: The wholesaler funding the project can approve the hours instead of the Board.
choices.why: Incorrect. The state Board, not a project sponsor, determines qualifying internship credit.

choices.text: Submit the project's written description to the Board for a credit determination.
choices.why: Correct. This is the process stated in 247 CMR 8.01(12).

questions.material_novelty: Tests approval of a previously unreviewed demonstration project rather than total experiential-hour requirements or interstate recognition.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the school has submitted the project and the Board accepts participation for credit, the stated approval defect disappears.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy intern works under the direct supervision of an on-premises registered pharmacist preceptor. The intern oversees two licensed technicians preparing routine prescriptions; the pharmacist performs final dispensing validation. Which statements correctly describe the duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The directly supervised pharmacy intern may supervise pharmacy technicians.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.01(15) expressly permits a directly supervised intern to supervise technicians.

choices.text: Once the intern supervises technicians, the intern may replace the pharmacist's final prescription check.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technician oversight by an intern is not a grant of independent pharmacist final-validation authority.

choices.text: The registered pharmacist remains responsible for final dispensing validation.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.04(1) retains that pharmacist duty.

choices.text: An intern who has completed four professional school years can work without a pharmacist preceptor when overseeing technicians.
choices.why: Incorrect. The applicable intern's authority under section 8.01(15) is expressly conditional on direct registered-preceptor supervision.

choices.text: The intern may authorize the technicians to give independent clinical drug counseling because they are under the intern's oversight.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.18(3) confines counseling to pharmacists and pharmacy interns.

questions.material_novelty: Asks whether supervised intern may supervise technicians, not whether the intern may counsel when the pharmacist leaves.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist preceptor leaves without a qualified substitute, section 8.01(15)'s direct-supervision condition is not met.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is checking identification badges before opening. Assume each worker's stated pharmacy credential is active. Which badge formats meet the specific Massachusetts personnel-title rules? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A licensed pharmacy intern wears the intern's name and the designation 'Pharmacy Intern'.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.01(14) requires the intern's name and that title.

choices.text: A licensed nationally certified pharmacy technician displays a first name and 'Certified Pharmacy Technician'.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.04(4)(a) specifies first name and certified technician title.

choices.text: A licensed noncertified pharmacy technician displays a first name and 'Pharmacy Technician'.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.02(6)(a) specifies this title.

choices.text: A licensed pharmacy technician trainee displays a first name and 'Pharmacy Technician Trainee'.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.03(4)(a) specifies this first name and title.

choices.text: An ordinary licensed technician without national certification can wear 'Certified Pharmacy Technician' whenever the pharmacist manager approves.
choices.why: Incorrect. Manager approval cannot confer the certified title without the Board-recognized certification requirements.

questions.material_novelty: Distinguishes the four role-specific legal badge titles rather than loss of certification or pharmacist identification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the fifth worker holds accepted national certification in addition to the technician license, the title may become appropriate.

questions.stem: A DEA-registered physician's authorized clinic assistant types a valid patient-specific paper Schedule IV prescription using information supplied by the physician. The assistant asks to sign the assistant's own name in the physician's signature space. There is no emergency exception. Which federal statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The assistant may prepare a prescription document for the physician's signature.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1306.05(f) expressly permits secretarial or agent preparation.

choices.text: The assistant may personally sign a controlled prescription in place of the prescribing practitioner whenever the clinic approves.
choices.why: Incorrect. Preparation authority under 1306.05(f) does not permit signing in place of the issuing practitioner.

choices.text: The physician remains responsible for ensuring the controlled prescription satisfies the applicable requirements.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.05(f) retains the issuing practitioner's responsibility.

choices.text: A pharmacist dispensing an improperly executed controlled prescription has no separate responsibility if the assistant typed it.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1306.05(f) expressly states that the dispensing pharmacist bears corresponding responsibility.

choices.text: The pharmacist must require the prescribing practitioner's legally adequate signature before treating this paper order as a valid prescription.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.05(d) requires practitioner manual signature for paper prescriptions where oral orders are not allowed, and 1306.05(f) does not displace that requirement.

questions.material_novelty: Separates agent document preparation from authorization of the practitioner signature; older questions mainly address changing existing signed prescriptions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A practitioner who personally signs the prepared valid paper prescription removes the missing-authentic-signature defect.

questions.stem: A clinician with valid Schedule II prescribing authority reviews an electronic prescription and marks it ready to sign. To save time, the clinician gives a clinic assistant the clinician's authentication credentials and asks the assistant to complete the two-factor authentication step. No emergency rule applies. What does 21 CFR 1311.140 require?

choices.text: The assistant's action legally signs the prescription because the clinician reviewed the record first.
choices.why: Incorrect. The signing authentication must be completed by the practitioner whose name and DEA registration appear.

choices.text: Any employee approved by the clinic's security officer may perform the signing authentication.
choices.why: Incorrect. Internal clinic approval cannot delegate the practitioner's personal authentication signature.

choices.text: The practitioner must personally complete the EPCS signing authentication.
choices.why: Correct. 1301.140(a)(3)–(6),(c) conditions signing and transmission on the named practitioner's own two-factor completion.

choices.text: A pharmacy technician can sign the order on receipt if the clinic did not authenticate it.
choices.why: Incorrect. A receiving technician cannot substitute for the prescriber's EPCS signature.

choices.text: The record becomes valid after the clinician confirms the assistant's act by telephone.
choices.why: Incorrect. Telephone confirmation does not replace the required EPCS signing mechanism.

questions.material_novelty: Tests who personally performs legal EPCS signature, not transmission-data truncation or whether the system can produce EPCS.
questions.counterfactual_flip: The named practitioner personally completes two-factor authentication in the compliant application.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives new outpatient prescriptions for several medications used in depression treatment. Which product is specifically a federal Schedule IV controlled substance, rather than an ordinary noncontrolled prescription medication?

choices.text: Zoloft (sertraline).
choices.why: Incorrect. Sertraline is an ordinary non-federally scheduled prescription antidepressant.

choices.text: Zurzuvae (zuranolone).
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(61) lists zuranolone in Schedule IV, and the FDA label explicitly states ZURZUVAE is Schedule IV.

choices.text: Wellbutrin (bupropion).
choices.why: Incorrect. Bupropion is not federally controlled.

choices.text: Prozac (fluoxetine).
choices.why: Incorrect. Fluoxetine is not federally controlled.

choices.text: Lexapro (escitalopram).
choices.why: Incorrect. Escitalopram is not federally controlled.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1308.14(c)(61); FDA ZURZUVAE Prescribing Information §9.1; 105 CMR 700.002(F)
questions.material_novelty: Tests an FDA-approved postpartum-depression drug (Zurzuvae/zuranolone), not previously present in any of A–D's 480 questions, against noncontrolled antidepressants; no repeat of the already-tested Soma/baclofen recognition.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the new order instead names an ordinary SSRI such as sertraline, federal Schedule IV controls do not attach.

questions.stem: A pharmacist is sorting new orders for clonidine, clonazepam (Klonopin), and clozapine in a Massachusetts outpatient pharmacy. Assuming standard prescription products and no unusual exemption, which schedule assignment is correct?

choices.text: Clonidine IV; clonazepam VI; clozapine IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. This reverses the federal controlled clonazepam classification and noncontrolled clonidine status.

choices.text: All three IV because their names begin with 'clon'.
choices.why: Incorrect. Similar spellings are not a legal basis for scheduling.

choices.text: Clonidine III; clonazepam II; clozapine V.
choices.why: Incorrect. None of these assignments matches the current federal scheduling regulations.

choices.text: All three VI because clozapine's former REMS requirement was discontinued.
choices.why: Incorrect. The FDA REMS history of clozapine has no bearing on federal Schedule IV clonazepam.

choices.text: Clonidine VI; clonazepam IV; clozapine VI.
choices.why: Correct. Clonazepam is a federal Schedule IV benzodiazepine; the other two are ordinary Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drugs.

questions.material_novelty: New clinically similar drug-name discrimination, not another Clozapine REMS enrollment question.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Replacing clonazepam with clonidine changes a Schedule IV dispensing obligation into an ordinary Schedule VI prescription.

questions.stem: A valid Schedule IV prescription was issued two months ago for 30 tablets with two authorized refills. Only one refill has been used. The ORIGINAL prescriber now orally authorizes two additional 30-tablet refills, and the pharmacist can document the call. There is no other restriction. Which statements reflect 21 CFR 1306.22(e)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Additional refills may be authorized on the original prescription if the overall limit remains five refills and six months from issue.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.22(e)(1) allows added authorization within both limits.

choices.text: An oral additional-refill authorization is always forbidden for Schedule IV prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1306.22(e) expressly allows oral authorizations within its conditions.

choices.text: The pharmacist must record the authorization's date, refill quantity, number of added refills and who received the authorization.
choices.why: Correct. This is required under 1306.22(e)(2).

choices.text: The new refill quantity must not exceed the quantity authorized for the original initial fill.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.22(e)(3) limits each added refill quantity.

choices.text: The patient may obtain a sixth refill merely by obtaining another telephone authorization against the same issued prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. The five-refill limit requires a new separate prescription for quantities beyond it.

questions.material_novelty: Tests original-prescriber additional refill authorization and its exact documentation/quantity conditions; previous cases focused on partial fills or refills already authorized.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If this would be a sixth refill, the original-prescription oral-addition pathway is unavailable and a new prescription is needed.

questions.stem: A HIPAA-covered pharmacy is paid by a manufacturer to use its prescription database to mail targeted advertising for a NEW, unrelated prescription drug. The payment is more than the expense of sending the mailing. The communication is not face-to-face and is not a refill reminder. No patient marketing authorization exists. What is required under 45 CFR 164.508?

choices.text: The pharmacy can proceed because all advertising for prescription drugs is treatment.
choices.why: Incorrect. Promotion of an unrelated drug for remuneration does not automatically qualify as treatment.

choices.text: The manufacturer may rely solely on the pharmacy's standard Notice of Privacy Practices.
choices.why: Incorrect. A general privacy notice is not a valid marketing authorization for this use of PHI.

choices.text: The pharmacy may proceed if its billing system confirms the patients have active health insurance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Insurance coverage does not authorize this PHI marketing use.

choices.text: Obtain a signed HIPAA marketing authorization that identifies the third-party manufacturer's financial remuneration before using these patients' PHI.
choices.why: Correct. Section 164.508(a)(3) generally requires authorization for marketing, with disclosure of third-party financial remuneration.

choices.text: The mailing is permitted without authorization because all drug advertising qualifies as a low-value promotional gift.
choices.why: Incorrect. A paid targeted mailing is not itself the nominal-value promotional gift exception.

questions.material_novelty: Tests paid patient-targeted marketing authorization, not ordinary treatment disclosures or a patient's own records access.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A genuine cost-limited refill reminder about a drug already prescribed could qualify for the distinct exception, unlike this paid unrelated promotion.

questions.topic: HIPAA access deadline and new-rule timing
questions.stem: On November 22, 2026, a HIPAA-covered pharmacy receives an authenticated patient's request for a copy of the patient's own electronic prescription records. A contracted business associate holds some of the records. HHS has recently published a final rule reducing future access deadlines, but that rule is not yet effective. Which statements describe the access obligation applicable to this request? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The newly announced 15-day rule already superseded the old deadline when published on November 19.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 2026 final rule is not effective until January 19, 2027, with a July 19, 2027 compliance date.

choices.text: The pharmacy must act on the access request within the existing 30-calendar-day outside limit.
choices.why: Correct. The existing 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)(i) governs a November 2026 request.

choices.text: If justified, the pharmacy may take one additional period of up to 30 calendar days after providing a timely written reason and completion date.
choices.why: Correct. Section 164.524(b)(2)(ii) permits one properly noticed extension.

choices.text: Waiting for the business associate to locate records does not restart the pharmacy's 30-day clock.
choices.why: Correct. HHS explains that the covered entity's deadline runs from receiving the request, even if records are at a business associate.

choices.text: The pharmacy may suspend all individual access requests until the new rule's 2027 compliance date.
choices.why: Incorrect. Existing access rights and timelines continue to apply.

questions.citation: 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2); 91 FR 74848 (November 19, 2026), effective January 19, 2027; compliance July 19, 2027
questions.material_novelty: New as-of-date gate distinguishes operative access deadline from the final rule that has been announced but is not yet effective, and tests BA timing.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the question is expressly set after the future compliance date, reverify and apply the 15-day rule instead.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts Schedule II prescription was written and signed on October 7. The pharmacist is applying the state's 30-day prescription-validity rule. For purposes of counting whether the prescription is within date, which date is day ONE?

choices.text: October 7, the day the prescriber signed the order.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.04(10) instructs the pharmacist to count the following day as day one.

choices.text: October 8, the day after the prescription was written.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.04(10) states this counting convention expressly.

choices.text: October 9, two days after signing.
choices.why: Incorrect. That would skip the first counted day.

choices.text: The patient's requested pickup date.
choices.why: Incorrect. A later pickup request does not reset the day-one issuance calculation.

choices.text: The date the pharmacy first enters the order in its computer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pharmacy processing date cannot replace the original issue date.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the specific Board counting convention, without reusing older delayed-dispensing or partial-fill scenarios.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the original issue date were October 8, day one would move to October 9.

questions.stem: A pharmacist reviews the electronic refill history of a valid Schedule IV prescription. The computer can retrieve the original prescription number and drug but may have omitted some refill-specific information. Which additional data must be retrievable under 21 CFR 1306.22(c)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The patient's personal preference for pharmacy text-message reminders.
choices.why: Incorrect. This preference is not an enumerated federal controlled-refill record element.

choices.text: The date of each fill or refill.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.22(c)(2) requires the date to be retrievable.

choices.text: The quantity dispensed on each refill.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.22(c)(3) expressly requires the dispensed quantity.

choices.text: The initials of the pharmacist who dispensed each refill.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.22(c)(4) requires dispensing-pharmacist initials.

choices.text: The exact number of tablets actually swallowed by the patient after each refill.
choices.why: Incorrect. Postdispensing patient adherence is not one of the specified federal pharmacy refill-history fields.

questions.material_novelty: Tests specific refill audit-trail fields, not whether another refill may be authorized or transferred.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the software also captures date, quantity, pharmacist initials and other required fields, this listed-record defect is repaired.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy lawfully substitutes a therapeutically interchangeable, lower-cost narrow-therapeutic-index immunosuppressant for a MassHealth patient's prescribed transplant medication. The prescriber did not prohibit interchange. Apart from ordinary substitution requirements, what special Massachusetts action applies?

choices.text: Notify FDA of each patient's drug substitution within 24 hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 12D assigns this patient-specific communication to the prescribing physician, not FDA.

choices.text: Obtain a new DEA Form 222 for the patient's noncontrolled immunosuppressant.
choices.why: Incorrect. DEA Form 222 applies to registrant Schedule II orders, not this generic substitution.

choices.text: The special transplant rule prohibits every eligible interchange, even with prescriber permission.
choices.why: Incorrect. The specified law requires prescriber notification when a substitution occurs; it is not phrased as an absolute ban.

choices.text: Notify the prescribing physician of the interchange.
choices.why: Correct. The final paragraph of M.G.L. c.112 §12D creates this additional prescriber notification obligation for MassHealth transplant patients.

choices.text: Only notify the prescriber if the patient is admitted to an intensive care unit.
choices.why: Incorrect. The trigger is MassHealth transplant narrow-therapeutic-index immunosuppressant substitution, not ICU admission.

questions.citation: M.G.L. c.112 §12D, final paragraph on MassHealth transplant immunosuppressants
questions.material_novelty: Tests MassHealth transplant-specific notice after a qualifying generic interchange, not the basic substitution mandate.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the drug is not a narrow-therapeutic-index immunosuppressant used for an organ/tissue transplant, the special final-paragraph notification may not apply.

questions.stem: A regulated seller handling lawful U.S. mail-order sales of pseudoephedrine products has already shipped 6.8 grams of pseudoephedrine BASE to one customer during the past 30 days. The same customer now orders another 1.0 gram. Today's order would not by itself exceed 3.6 grams, and no special exemption applies. What should the seller do?

choices.text: Ship it because the ordinary retail monthly ceiling is nine grams.
choices.why: Incorrect. Regulated mail-order sellers have a separate, lower 7.5-gram per-30-day ceiling.

choices.text: Ship it if the customer again supplies valid identification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Identity verification does not waive the 7.5-gram mail-order ceiling.

choices.text: Do not complete this order: it would bring this customer's 30-day mail-order pseudoephedrine total to 7.8 grams, exceeding the 7.5-gram limit.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1314.100(b) imposes the mail-order 7.5-gram limit, independent of the daily 3.6-gram rule.

choices.text: Refuse every future pseudoephedrine order from this customer permanently.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation uses rolling daily/30-day quantity windows, not a permanent prohibition after an attempted excess purchase.

choices.text: Complete the purchase by labeling the package 'prescription only'.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing the package label does not exempt a regulated mail-order sale from federal quantity limits.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the mail-order-specific 7.5-gram window rather than the already-tested ordinary in-person retail limit.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If prior qualifying mail-order sales were 6.0 grams, the new 1.0-gram order would not violate this 30-day limit, assuming other rules pass.

questions.topic: Emergency use of brand in generic interchange
questions.stem: A Massachusetts prescription names a brand drug and does not say 'no substitution.' Normally a less expensive interchangeable generic is required. During a documented MEDICAL EMERGENCY, the pharmacy has none of the cheaper interchangeables in stock but does have the prescribed brand. The purchaser is willing to accept a permitted deviation in writing. Which actions or conditions are supported by 247 CMR 9.05(1)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Dispensing the brand must be delayed in all cases until a less expensive interchangeable generic arrives.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board regulation expressly provides a medical-emergency exception when no less expensive interchangeable product is in stock.

choices.text: The pharmacist may dispense the prescribed brand during this qualifying emergency.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.05(1)(a) permits the brand in this precise no-generic-in-stock emergency situation.

choices.text: The pharmacist may change the brand to any unrelated medicine with similar therapeutic use without prescriber approval.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception is for the specific brand/interchangeable product relationship, not arbitrary therapeutic substitution.

choices.text: The pharmacist must record the date, hour and nature of the medical emergency.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.05(1)(b) specifies all three documentation facts.

choices.text: The purchaser must indicate acceptance of the deviation from the ordinary interchange rule in writing.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.05(1)(b) separately requires written purchaser acceptance.

questions.material_novelty: Reverse of the previously tested 'no substitution, brand unavailable, dispense generic' case: here generic interchange is ordinarily mandated but emergency stock permits the prescribed brand.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the less expensive interchangeable generic is in stock and no separate exception applies, the medical-emergency stock exception for using the higher-priced brand is not established.

questions.stem: A DEA-registered retail pharmacy wants to store its controlled-substance shipping invoices, executed paper DEA Forms 222 and original inventories at a distant corporate record center. The pharmacy is considering the central-recordkeeping mechanism in 21 CFR 1304.04. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Certain financial and shipping records may be kept centrally under the prescribed DEA notification procedure, unless the DEA denies the arrangement.
choices.why: Correct. 1304.04(a)(1) allows this specifically limited category after required notice and 14 days following DEA receipt unless denied.

choices.text: Executed DEA Forms 222 may automatically leave the registered location because they can be scanned.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1304.04(b)(1) expressly excludes executed order forms from the central-recordkeeping exception.

choices.text: Required controlled-substance inventories must remain at each registered location under this exception.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1304.04(b)(1) excludes inventories from central offsite files.

choices.text: An approved central records system must make requested records available at the registered location within two business days after DEA's written request.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1304.04(b)(3) provides the two-business-day production duty.

choices.text: Once the corporate location is approved, a pharmacy may routinely delete all underlying controlled-drug records before two years.
choices.why: Incorrect. Central storage does not waive the federal minimum two-year record retention requirement.

questions.material_novelty: Separates eligible offsite financial/shipping files from executed order forms/inventories and verifies DEA central-location notice/production conditions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only properly notified shipping invoices are moved and signed order forms/inventories remain at the registered location, the core conflict is removed.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy ordered ten commercial containers of a Schedule II drug using a valid paper DEA Form 222. The supplier delivered SEVEN containers on November 9 and the remaining THREE on November 15, within the federal order period. What must the purchaser record on its own Form 222 copy?

choices.text: One entry showing ten containers on the original ordering date, whether or not received then.
choices.why: Incorrect. 1305.13(e) requires actual received quantities and their corresponding receipt dates.

choices.text: Seven containers received November 9 and three containers received November 15.
choices.why: Correct. The purchaser records the number furnished on each line and the date each shipment was received.

choices.text: Only the supplier's shipping dates; the purchaser has no separate receipt documentation duty.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1305.13(e) assigns the receiving record to the purchaser.

choices.text: The quantity delivered may be omitted after the second shipment arrives in full.
choices.why: Incorrect. Completion of the total order does not cancel the recordkeeping requirement.

choices.text: Record one quantity of ten on November 15, even though seven were received six days earlier.
choices.why: Incorrect. Recording all ten as received on the last date would not accurately document the earlier seven containers.

questions.material_novelty: Tests purchaser's actual receipt dates and quantities for separate shipments, rather than the supplier's 60-day shipment limit.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If all ten containers arrived together on November 15, a single ten-container receipt-date entry would describe the shipment accurately.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy transfers intact tablets from the manufacturer's original stock bottle into a clean bulk STOCK container for pharmacy use, not into patient-specific dispensing packaging. Which data must the new container's label include under 247 CMR 9.19(5)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacy's marketing slogan in place of the product identification details.
choices.why: Incorrect. A slogan cannot substitute for the required product and traceability fields.

choices.text: The medication's name and strength or concentration.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(5) expressly requires these identifying fields.

choices.text: The drug's NDC and manufacturer or supplier.
choices.why: Correct. Both are included in the Board's required stock-container label elements.

choices.text: The lot number and assigned expiration date.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(5) retains these stability/traceability identifiers.

choices.text: The date the medication was moved out of the original manufacturer bottle.
choices.why: Correct. This transfer date is separately required for other stock containers.

questions.material_novelty: Tests relocated BULK stock labeling and traceability, rather than prescription containers handed to patients or generic-interchange labels.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the stock remains in its fully identified original manufacturer's stock bottle, the special re-containering documentation problem does not arise.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts drug store pharmacy occupies a secured section inside a large supermarket. A wholesaler arrives with sealed Schedule II STOCK cartons, but the pharmacist is occupied. The driver proposes leaving the shipment at the supermarket's ordinary receiving desk for store staff to bring into the pharmacy later. What does 247 CMR 9.21(7) require?

choices.text: Arrange delivery of the controlled-stock cartons directly to the pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. All drug-order deliveries containing controlled substances must be delivered directly to the pharmacy under 247 CMR 9.21(7).

choices.text: Leave the cartons at the supermarket receiving desk if a cashier signs for the outer box.
choices.why: Incorrect. A retail cashier's signature does not replace the requirement for controlled-drug orders to be delivered directly to the pharmacy.

choices.text: Treat the supermarket's general receiving room as the pharmacy because it is in the same building.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(7) calls for delivery to the pharmacy, not simply the same retail building.

choices.text: Allow delivery through any package-locker service as long as the shipment remains sealed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule does not establish a sealed-parcel exception for controlled stock orders.

choices.text: Redirect the cartons to a patient's workplace because home or worksite delivery rules also cover pharmacy stock.
choices.why: Incorrect. Rules for patient-specific prescription delivery do not replace pharmacy stock acquisition security.

questions.material_novelty: Contrasts WHOLESALER STOCK delivery to pharmacy against existing questions on last-mile patient prescription delivery and pharmacy-within-store alarms.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the carrier brings the shipment directly to the pharmacy's authorized receiving process, the wholesale stock-delivery issue is resolved.
